channel.title: ThePickLog — verdicts & field notes
channel.description: We test what's being sold to traders. Rules frozen before the fact, graded forward against a control, verdicts published either way — starting with our own strategy, which failed.

item.title: Experiment 12: can an AI judge forecast a drawdown better than four numbers?
item.description: Two pinned AI judges — a filing reader and a general model from a different company — graded forward on whether they forecast a 20% drawdown better than the plain score they both see. Registered 2026-10-25 before the first window pick; window 26 Oct to 31 Dec 2026; one verdict look on or after 2027-01-11, published either way.

item.title: Experiments 06–09 published: four retail techniques, one verdict date
item.description: The Supertrend flip, the moving-average pullback, Bollinger Band mean reversion and NR7 volatility contraction — four techniques currently taught and sold to retail traders, registered together on 2026-08-06 and running forward on 40 large caps against a day-matched control. Each gets one verdict look on 2026-11-02, corrected for multiple testing across the eight experiments running at once.

item.title: Experiment 05 registered: does the market only make money while it's closed?
item.description: Split every trading day into its overnight leg and its intraday leg. Across 27 years of QQQ, essentially all of the return came from the overnight leg — $1 compounded overnight-only grew to about $35 while intraday-only fell to 47 cents. Firms turned this into ETFs; the ETFs died. An attribution claim, not a trading claim, with the verdict locked to a single pre-declared date.

item.title: Experiment 04 registered: does the turn-of-month effect exist?
item.description: One of the oldest claims in the calendar-effect literature — returns clustering at the turn of each month — in journals since the 1980s and still sold in seasonality newsletters. The window was frozen before the fact and is graded forward on QQQ. It comes out of an exploratory sweep of 25 calendar patterns in which, corrected for multiple testing, none survived.

item.title: About ThePickLog — who runs this, and why he tested his own strategy first
item.description: The operator, the standard the site applies (define the rule before the outcome is known, test forward, compare to a pre-specified benchmark, publish either way), and why the first strategy tested was his own — which failed.

item.title: Correction: we logged 128 picks after the opening bell
item.description: The record rests on picks being written down before the market opens. On seven sessions our scheduler drifted past the bell and logged anyway — and an outside reader found it in our public CSV before we did. 128 picks excluded, headline restated −2.68% → −3.40%, and a hard pre-open gate so it cannot recur.

item.title: Field note: the bug that makes your backtest look good
item.description: Price history is silently rewritten every time a company splits. Mix a stored price with a re-downloaded one and you invent returns that never happened — and in cheap stocks the error is always in your favour. We found it in our own code, where it had turned a −2.9% baseline into +8.0%. Six checks that catch it.

item.title: Experiment 03 registered: is the MACD bullish crossover profitable?
item.description: The most widely taught indicator signal in retail trading, frozen as an exact rule with a day-matched control before any of the data it will be judged on exists. Registered prior: no edge — roughly 1 in 6 that it clears.

item.title: Experiment 02 registered: does the 2-period RSI strategy actually work?
item.description: One of the most published retail setups of the last twenty years, almost always sold on its win rate. We're testing whether a high win rate survives contact with expectancy — on liquid names, where costs can't be blamed for the answer. Verdict on or after 2 November 2026 (date fixed 2026-08-28, before any outcome was read).

item.title: Experiment 01 verdict: we tested our own stock screener. It lost money.
item.description: We pre-registered the edge we believed in and ran it forward for seven weeks. It failed — significantly, in the opposite direction to our prediction. n=309, −3.0pp versus baseline, 95% CI [−4.4, −1.5]. At 30 trades it looked like it worked; that early read was noise.
